blocks.text: Roslyakova belongs to what fashion press term the "Wide Eyed Doll" era of modeling of the mid-to-late 2000s, alongside models such as Sasha Pivovarova, Jessica Stam, and Gemma Ward, whose large-eyed, doll-like look forms part of the visual basis for the aesthetic.

The aesthetic was revived as a named internet aesthetic roughly a decade and a half after the original show, spreading through TikTok edits and Pinterest boards built specifically around images from the Galliano show and Roslyakova's runway career. Within this community the aesthetic is frequently discussed alongside the broader "Slavic Doll" hashtag cluster, and TikTok users have paired Roslyakova's runway footage with other 2000s-era "doll-faced" models such as Snejana Onopka and Ruslana Korshunova. The name has occasionally been confused with Disney's 2013 film Frozen in unrelated content, such as ballet productions combining Hans Christian Andersen's "The Snow Queen" with the film's music, though this overlap is coincidental rather than a source of the aesthetic's visual style.

The aesthetic is inspired by the styling from the original Galliano show: models' heads are covered in tight caps that erase the hairline, giving a bald, doll-like silhouette, over which sit heavy veils and headpieces made of layered gold or silver coins and pearls, often extending down over the forehead and around the neck like a collar. Pat McGrath's original makeup for the show used dark, smudged eye makeup that appears to run or melt down the cheekbones, contrasted against extremely pale, almost bloodless-looking skin, an effect frequently reproduced in fan-made makeup tutorials circulating under the aesthetic's name. Garments draw on both bridal and Slavic folk costume references simultaneously, pairing sheer white tulle gowns with embroidered panels, high fur-trimmed collars, and dark gold-trimmed jackets inspired by traditional Russian and Ukrainian dress.

Community-curated moodboards for the aesthetic extend beyond the runway photography itself to include winter photography of snow-covered Orthodox churches, statuary, and forests, as well as illustrated fantasy imagery of ice queens and stylized sketches of Russian folk dress, suggesting the aesthetic is read by its community as broader than a single fashion show and closer to a wintery, Slavic-coded fantasy of femininity.
